Intensity level is **10 log₁₀(I/I₀)**, with I₀ = 10⁻¹² W m⁻².
**Step 1 — write the definition.**
L = **10 log₁₀(I/I₀)** ✓
**Step 2 — form the ratio.**
I/I₀ = 10⁻⁸/10⁻¹²
= **10⁴** ✓
**Step 3 — take the logarithm.**
log₁₀(10⁴) = **4** ✓
**Step 4 — multiply by ten.**
L = 10 x 4 = **40 dB** ✓
**Why I₀ = 10⁻¹² W m⁻².** It is the **threshold of hearing** at 1 kHz ✓ a sound so faint
that the eardrum moves less than the diameter of an atom. Choosing it as the reference
makes 0 dB the quietest audible sound.
**Why the scale is logarithmic.** The audible range spans **twelve** orders of magnitude
in intensity ✓ from 10⁻¹² to about 1 W m⁻² at the threshold of pain. A linear scale would
be unusable; the logarithm compresses it to 0-120 dB, and happens to match the ear's own
response.
**Where 40 dB sits.** A **quiet library** or soft background music ✓ Conversation is
about 60 dB, a vacuum cleaner 70 dB, a pneumatic drill 100 dB.
**The ten-decibel rule.** Each **10 dB** means a factor of **ten** in intensity ✓ so
40 dB is 10⁴ times the threshold, and 80 dB would be 10⁸ times - ten thousand times more
intense than this sound, not merely twice as much.
**Why loudness and intensity level are not the same.** Perceived loudness roughly
**doubles** for every 10 dB ✓ so a 40 dB sound seems about **16** times as loud as the
threshold, though it is 10000 times as intense.
**The amplitude.** Since I ∝ a²,
a/a₀ = √(10⁴) = **100** ✓ The pressure amplitude is a hundred times the threshold value
of about 2 x 10⁻⁵ Pa, so roughly **2 x 10⁻³ Pa** - still a tiny fraction of atmospheric
pressure.
**Why the decibel is dimensionless.** It is the logarithm of a **ratio** ✓ which is why
a reference level must always be stated; "40 dB" alone is meaningless without I₀.
**The common slip.** Using **20** log₁₀ instead of 10 log₁₀ ✓ The factor 20 applies to
**pressure or amplitude** ratios, the factor 10 to **intensity** ratios - and since
I ∝ p², the two give the same decibel figure when used correctly.
**Reading the distractors.** **4** ✗ forgets the factor of ten. **80** ✗ uses 20 log₁₀ on
an intensity. **8** ✗ matches no step ✓
∴ 40.

Read ω and k straight off the equation, then λ = 2π/k and v = ω/k.
**Step 1 — expand the argument.**
y = 0·05 sin π(2t − 0·02x)
= 0·05 sin(**2πt** − **0·02πx**) ✓
**Step 2 — identify ω and k.** Comparing with y = a sin(ωt − kx):
ω = **2π rad s⁻¹** ✓
k = **0·02π rad m⁻¹** ✓
**Step 3 — find the wavelength.** Two particles **in phase** are one wavelength apart:
λ = 2π/k = 2π/0·02π
= **100 m** ✓
**Step 4 — find the wave velocity.**
v = ω/k = 2π/0·02π
= **100 m s⁻¹** ✓
**The check by v = fλ.**
f = ω/2π = **1 Hz** ✓
v = fλ = 1 x 100 = **100 m s⁻¹** ✓ the same, as it must be.
**Why "in phase" means one wavelength apart.** Particles separated by λ differ in phase
by **2π** ✓ which is no difference at all - they move identically, rising and falling
together. The **minimum** such separation is one full wavelength.
**The companion question.** Particles in **antiphase** - exactly out of step - are
**λ/2 = 50 m** apart ✓ which is where the first distractor comes from.
**Why the π must be distributed first.** Written as π(2t − 0·02x), the coefficients are
**not** ω and k ✓ Failing to multiply through is the commonest error here, and gives
ω = 2, k = 0·02, hence a wavelength of 314 m.
**What the other quantities are.**
amplitude **0·05 m** ✓
period T = 2π/ω = **1 s** ✓
frequency **1 Hz** ✓
**Why the minus sign matters.** y = a sin(ωt − kx) travels in the **+x** direction ✓ A
plus sign would mean propagation towards −x. The sign tells the direction, not the
speed.
**Why this is a slow, long wave.** 1 Hz and 100 m ✓ far too low in frequency for sound
in air; more like a wave on a long heavy rope or a swell at sea.
**The general relation worth remembering.**
v = **ω/k** = **fλ** = **λ/T** ✓ three forms of the same statement, and any of them
serves.
**Reading the distractors.** **50 m, 50 m s⁻¹** ✗ halves both - it uses the antiphase
separation and then errs again. **50 m, 100 m s⁻¹** ✗ gets the velocity right but uses
the antiphase distance ✓
∴ 100 m, 100 ms⁻¹.

The wall acts as an image source approaching at the same speed, so the beat frequency
is **2uf/(v − u)**.
**Step 1 — see what the listener hears.** Two sounds ✓
the **direct** note from the fork he carries, unshifted at **338 Hz** - fork and ear
move together ✓
the **reflected** note from the wall, Doppler-shifted ✓
**Step 2 — treat the reflection.** The wall reflects the sound, and the listener is
**approaching** the reflected wavefronts while the **source** also approaches the wall ✓
The standard result is that the wall behaves as an **image** of the fork, moving towards
the observer at **2u**... but handled as two separate shifts it comes to the same thing:
f′ = f(v + u)/(v − u) ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
f′ = 338(340 + 2)/(340 − 2)
= 338 x 342/338 ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
= **342 Hz** ✓
**Step 5 — find the beats.**
beat frequency = 342 − 338 = **4 per second** ✓
**The neat cancellation.** Because f = 338 and v − u = 338, the arithmetic collapses
exactly ✓ The question is constructed so that f′ = v + u = 342 - a deliberate
convenience worth spotting.
**The general formula.**
beats = f′ − f = f[(v + u)/(v − u) − 1] = **2uf/(v − u)** ✓
= 2(2)(338)/338 = **4** ✓ confirming the answer directly.
**Why there are two shifts, not one.** Going **to** the wall, the fork is a moving
source: the wall receives fv/(v − u) ✓ Coming **back**, the listener is a moving
observer approaching that re-radiated sound: multiply by (v + u)/v ✓ The v cancels,
leaving f(v + u)/(v − u).
**Why the direct sound is not shifted.** Source and observer move **together**, with no
relative velocity ✓ so the ear receives the fork's true 338 Hz.
**Why beats are heard at all.** Two slightly different frequencies alternately reinforce
and cancel ✓ at the **difference** frequency - here a slow throb four times a second,
easily counted.
**A practical note.** This is the basis of **Doppler sonar** and of ultrasonic
blood-flow measurement ✓ where the reflected signal's shift reveals the reflector's
speed.
**What happens if he walks away.** The signs reverse: f′ = f(v − u)/(v + u) = **334 Hz**
✓ and the beat frequency is again about 4 - though the reflected note is now **lower**
than the direct one.
**Reading the distractors.** **2** ✗ counts only one of the two Doppler shifts. **6** ✗
and **8** ✗ overcount them ✓
∴ 4.

Energy and wavelength are **inversely** proportional, so a third of the energy gives
**three times** the wavelength.
**Step 1 — find the first transition's energy.**
3E → E: ΔE₁ = **2E** ✓
and ΔE₁ = hc/λ, so **2E = hc/λ** ✓
**Step 2 — find the second transition's energy.**
5E/3 → E: ΔE₂ = 5E/3 − E = **2E/3** ✓
**Step 3 — compare.**
ΔE₂/ΔE₁ = (2E/3)/(2E) = **1/3** ✓
**Step 4 — invert for the wavelength.** Since λ = hc/ΔE,
λ′/λ = ΔE₁/ΔE₂ = **3**
λ′ = **3λ** ✓
**Why the inverse relation.** λ = **hc/E** ✓ A smaller energy gap means a less energetic
photon, a lower frequency and therefore a **longer** wavelength. The transition with a
third of the energy emits a photon of three times the wavelength.
**The numbers made concrete.** Suppose E = 1 eV:
3E → E emits **2 eV**, λ = 1240/2 = **620 nm** - orange ✓
5E/3 → E emits **0·667 eV**, λ = 1240/0·667 = **1860 nm** - infrared ✓
and 1860/620 = **3** ✓
**The convenient constant.** hc = **1240 eV nm** ✓ so λ(nm) = 1240/E(eV) - worth
memorising, and it turns such questions into one division.
**Why only differences matter.** The photon carries away **ΔE**, not the absolute level ✓
which is why the zero of energy can be chosen anywhere without affecting any spectral
line.
**Why atomic spectra are line spectra.** The levels are **discrete**, so only certain
ΔE are available ✓ Each gives one sharp wavelength, and the pattern of lines identifies
the element - the basis of spectroscopy and of the discovery of helium in the sun.
**The third possible transition here.**
3E → 5E/3: ΔE = **4E/3** ✓ giving λ″ = 3λ/2. Note that this plus the 5E/3 → E photon
accounts exactly for the 3E → E photon's energy: 4E/3 + 2E/3 = 2E ✓ - the **Ritz
combination principle**, and a good check on any level diagram.
**Why the wavelengths do not simply add.** Energies add; wavelengths do not ✓
1/λ is the additive quantity, which is why spectroscopists work in **wavenumbers**,
cm⁻¹.
**Reading the distractors.** **5λ** ✗ uses the level 5E/3 rather than the gap.
**3λ/5** ✗ and **2λ** ✗ invert or mis-form the ratio ✓ Computing both gaps and dividing
avoids every trap.
∴ 3 λ.

An open pipe gives **all** harmonics of v/2L; find which one is 1·1 kHz.
**Step 1 — find the fundamental.**
f₁ = v/2L = 330/(2 x 0·30) ✓
= 330/0·60
= **550 Hz** ✓
**Step 2 — write the harmonic series.** An open pipe supports **every** integer
multiple ✓
550, **1100**, 1650, 2200 Hz ...
**Step 3 — locate 1100 Hz.**
1100/550 = **2** ✓ the **second harmonic**.
**Why an open pipe gives all harmonics.** Both ends are **antinodes** of displacement ✓
so the condition is L = nλ/2 for every integer n, and f_n = nv/2L. A **closed** pipe,
with a node at one end, gives only the **odd** harmonics.
**The second harmonic's picture.** L = λ, so λ = **0·30 m** ✓ with antinodes at both
ends and at the centre, and **two** nodes a quarter-length in from each end.
**Check by wavelength.**
λ = v/f = 330/1100 = **0·30 m** ✓ exactly the pipe length, as the second harmonic
requires.
**Harmonic versus overtone.** The second **harmonic** is the **first** overtone ✓ The
numbering differs by one, and questions exploit the confusion. "Harmonic" counts from
the fundamental as the first; "overtone" counts the fundamental as none.
**Why the closed pipe would fail here.** Its fundamental would be v/4L = **275 Hz**, with
harmonics at 275, 825, 1375 ✓ - 1100 Hz is **not** among them, since it is an even
multiple.
**Why an open pipe sounds richer.** It contains both odd and even harmonics ✓ which is
why a flute (open) and a clarinet (effectively closed) have such different timbres at
the same pitch, the clarinet's odd-harmonic spectrum giving its hollow tone.
**The end correction, in practice.** The antinode lies slightly **outside** the open
end, by about **0·6r** ✓ so the effective length exceeds 30 cm a little and the real
frequencies are marginally lower. The question ignores it, as school problems do.
**Why the speed of sound is given.** It depends on **temperature**: v = 331√(T/273) ✓
330 m s⁻¹ corresponds to about 0-1 °C. A warm room would give 343 m s⁻¹ and shift the
harmonics up by 4%.
**Reading the distractors.** **Fifth**, **fourth** and **third** harmonics ✗ would be
2750, 2200 and 1650 Hz ✓ Dividing 1100 by the fundamental settles it at once.
∴ Second harmonic.

The tuned circuit resonates at **f = 1/(2π√(LC))**, so √(LC) = 1/(2πf).
**Step 1 — write the resonance condition.**
f = **1/(2π√(LC))** ✓
**Step 2 — rearrange.**
√(LC) = **1/(2πf)** ✓
**Step 3 — substitute f = 2 MHz.**
√(LC) = 1/(2π x 2 x 10⁶)
= **1/(4π x 10⁶)** ✓
**The numerical value.**
= 1/(1·257 x 10⁷) = **7·96 x 10⁻⁸ s** ✓ Note that √(LC) has the dimensions of **time** -
it is the circuit's natural time constant, and 1/√(LC) is its angular frequency.
**Why a carrier of 2 MHz.** It lies in the **medium-wave** broadcast band ✓ Modulating a
3 kHz speech signal onto it requires a bandwidth of only 6 kHz - a third of a per cent
of the carrier - so hundreds of stations can share the band without overlapping.
**Why the carrier must be high.** Three reasons ✓
**antenna size**: an efficient antenna is about **λ/4**. At 3 kHz, λ = 100 km; at 2 MHz,
λ = 150 m and λ/4 = **37·5 m** - a tall mast, but buildable.
**multiplexing**: different carriers keep stations separate.
**range**: low frequencies radiate very inefficiently from any practical antenna.
**What the tuned circuit does.** The **LC** combination oscillates naturally at this
frequency ✓ and the amplifier sustains the oscillation, generating a steady sinusoidal
carrier onto which the audio is impressed.
**A plausible pair of component values.** With C = 100 pF:
L = (7·96 x 10⁻⁸)²/10⁻¹⁰ = **63·3 µH** ✓ an entirely ordinary coil - a few dozen turns
on a ferrite core.
**The quality factor.** A sharp tuned circuit has high **Q = ωL/R** ✓ which keeps the
carrier pure and, in the receiver, rejects adjacent stations.
**Why amplitude modulation.** The carrier's **amplitude** follows the message:
c_m(t) = (A_c + A_m sin ω_m t) sin ω_c t ✓ producing sidebands at f_c ± f_m. It is simple
to generate and to detect with a diode, which is why AM broadcasting came first.
**The modulation index.** µ = A_m/A_c ✓ kept below 1 to avoid distortion;
overmodulation clips the envelope and the recovered audio is ruined.
**Reading the distractors.** **1/(2π x 10⁶)** ✗ uses f = 1 MHz. **1/(2 x 10⁶)** ✗ drops
the 2π entirely, and **1/(3π x 10⁶)** ✗ matches no step ✓
∴ 1/(4π × 10⁶).

Filing **raises** A's frequency; since the beats **increase**, A must have been **above**
B already.
**Step 1 — use the beat frequency.** 4 beats with B = 384 Hz means
f_A = **380 Hz** or **388 Hz** ✓
**Step 2 — recall the effect of filing.** Removing material from the prong **raises** the
frequency ✓ (Loading with wax lowers it.)
**Step 3 — test f_A = 380 Hz.** Filing raises it towards 384, so the beats would
**fall** to 3, 2, 1, 0 ✗ The question says they increase. **Rejected**.
**Step 4 — test f_A = 388 Hz.** Filing raises it to 389, 390, ... and the difference from
384 **grows**: 5, 6, ... ✓ Consistent.
**Step 5 — conclude.** f_A = **388 Hz** ✓
**Why beats alone are ambiguous.** The beat frequency is **|f₁ − f₂|** ✓ a modulus, so
4 beats admits two answers. A second observation - loading, filing, or changing the
tension - is always needed to resolve it.
**The companion rule.** If the beats had **decreased** on filing, A would have been the
**lower** fork, 380 Hz ✓ Reading that one word correctly is the whole question.
**The alternative test.** Attach a small piece of **wax** to a prong of A ✓ This lowers
A's frequency. If the beats then increase, A was below B; if they decrease, A was above.
Either experiment serves.
**Why filing raises the frequency.** For a tuning fork f ∝ **t/l²** ✓ with t the prong
thickness and l its length, so filing the **tips** shortens l and raises f. This is how
forks are tuned at the factory.
**Why 384 Hz.** It is **G** above middle C in the scientific scale, where C = 256 Hz ✓
and 384 = 256 x 3/2, a perfect fifth - which is why such numbers recur in these
questions.
**How beats are heard.** Superposing two waves of nearby frequency gives an amplitude
envelope varying at the **difference** frequency ✓
y = 2a cos(π Δf t) sin(2π f̄ t)
with the ear detecting **two** loudness maxima per cycle of the cosine, hence Δf beats
per second.
**Why the ear cannot follow fast beats.** Above about **10 per second** they merge into a
sensation of roughness, and above 20 the ear begins to hear a separate difference tone ✓
**Where this is used.** Piano and organ tuning, tuning a guitar against a reference, and
checking a fork against a sonometer ✓ Nulling the beats is far more sensitive than
comparing pitches by ear.
**Reading the distractors.** **380 Hz** ✗ is the answer if the beats had **decreased** -
the intended trap. **379** and **389 Hz** ✗ would give 5 beats, not 4 ✓
∴ 388 Hz.
